Buying cartridges at the destination

A Parcours de Chasse – Sporting™ or Compak® Sporting competition needs hundreds of cartridges, but airline limits allow only a few boxes: see Flying with a gun. So cartridges are usually bought at the destination: in the ground's shop, from a local dealer or through the organiser, who often has a supplier.

Order cartridges in advance, especially if you need a particular brand, a particular load (the weight of shot in the cartridge) or 20 gauge. Popular cartridges can run out during a big competition. Ask where and when you can collect them.

Buying cartridges is governed by law too. In many countries the seller asks to see a gun permit, the European Firearms Pass or a temporary permit. The rules for foreigners can differ from those for locals, so check with the organiser or the ground.

FITASC competitions have cartridge rules, the same in both disciplines. A cartridge may hold at most 28 g of lead shot (up to 2% more is tolerated). The shot must be round pellets of one size, 2.0 to 2.5 mm across (±0.1 mm). Not allowed: reloads (cartridges refilled at home) and dispersers (inserts that make the shot spread wider). Also banned: mixed shot (pellets of different sizes or kinds in one cartridge), black powder and tracers (cartridges that show the path of the shot) (Chapter 7 · Cartridge rules, Chapter 18 · Prohibited ammunition).

Where this is in the rules: Chapter 18 · Cartridges: 28 g lead, shot 2-2.5 mm

Read the label on the box, and try unfamiliar cartridges in practice before the competition. More about loads: Load weight.

Some grounds allow only steel shot or other lead-free shot, because of environmental rules. Steel does not suit all guns and chokes. Look on the barrels for a proof mark for steel shot (small stamped marks that show what the gun was tested for), and ask a gunsmith (Steel shot and chokes). Ask about such limits before the trip: they can apply on practice days too.

Work out how many cartridges you need, with a small margin. Taking leftovers home can be difficult, and in many countries you may not sell or hand cartridges to another person, so check the local law first. At the hotel, store cartridges as the country's rules require, and do not leave them in the car.

Key points

  • Competition cartridges are usually bought at the destination: order ahead.
  • Buying may need documents: check the local rules.
  • FITASC rules: at most 28 g of lead shot (up to 2% more is tolerated), and no reloads.
  • Some grounds allow steel shot only: check your gun and chokes.
  • Work out the quantity so that little is left over.

Did you know?

A steel pellet is about 30% lighter than a lead pellet of the same size, so it loses speed faster in flight.

Check yourself · 3 questions

  1. Why are competition cartridges usually bought at the destination?

    1. Because FITASC asks for cartridges from the host
    2. Because cartridges are always cheaper abroad
    3. Because airlines allow only a few boxes
    Answer

    Because airlines allow only a few boxes

    Baggage allows only a few kilograms of cartridges, and a competition needs hundreds of them.

  2. What is the most shot a cartridge may hold under the FITASC rules?

    1. 28 g of lead, with a +2% tolerance
    2. 24 g of lead, with no tolerance
    3. 32 g of lead, with a +5% tolerance
    Answer

    28 g of lead, with a +2% tolerance

    In both disciplines the limit is 28 g of lead with a +2% tolerance.

    Chapter 7 · Cartridge rules

  3. A ground allows steel shot only. What should you check?

    1. Whether the shop sells reloaded cartridges
    2. Whether your gun and chokes suit steel
    3. Whether lead is still fine for practice
    Answer

    Whether your gun and chokes suit steel

    Steel shot does not suit all guns and chokes, so check in advance.
